text:
The father knows that paying the ransom would not save his daughter but would doom her. The call is not a straightforward exchange of money for a life: the act of producing and handing over one hundred million yen would reveal something to the kidnapper—most centrally that the daughter can identify him—and that revelation would lead the kidnapper to kill her to silence her. So payment would trigger her death rather than prevent it.

At the same time, the father understands that he himself is the person the kidnapper is really after. The demand is aimed at drawing the father into the kidnapper's power, and paying would not only endanger the daughter but also put at risk another specific person whose life is tied to whether the money is paid; the kidnapper would turn on that person or on the daughter as a result. Thus paying would cost more lives than it could possibly save.

Therefore the father concludes that the ransom must not be paid. He intends to save his daughter by some route other than paying the kidnapper's price, and in doing so he hopes to protect both her and the other person at risk. Refusing to pay keeps the kidnapper from gaining whatever the payment would unlock.

text:
The captive is not the daughter but her father: he is the one the kidnapper is holding, and the threat "this hostage dies" refers to him. His daughter, still free, is the one phoning—her voice is genuinely hers—conveying the kidnapper's demand: bring one hundred million yen alone by noon tomorrow, or the father dies; no police.

Hearing this, the father realizes why the ransom must not be paid. He already believes that even if the money were handed over, the kidnapper will kill the witnesses who could identify him, so payment would not save him; the money itself is not the kidnapper's real aim. More decisively, the demand is that the money be brought alone—and since the father is the one in captivity, the only person who could deliver it is his free daughter. Paying would therefore draw her alone into the kidnapper's hands, making her a second captive, and because she too could identify the kidnapper, she would be killed as a witness. Payment would thus turn the kidnapper loose against the rest of his family rather than protect them.

So the father makes the self-sacrificing choice: refusing the ransom keeps his daughter and family out of the kidnapper's reach and denies the kidnapper his reward, even though it means accepting his own likely death. That is why, hearing the demand, he decides the ransom should not be paid.

checkpoints.reason: Protective refusal is present, but the submission omits explicit communication that she must not pay or come and does not clearly accept danger to his own life.
The daughter's wealth is not stated or entailed.
The daughter's status as his only family is not stated or entailed.

contradictions.quote: he knows the money cannot save him: the kidnapper is with him and will kill the hostage regardless of payment
contradictions.reference: The explanation concerns the father’s fear and decision; it does not establish that the kidnapper eventually kills either of them. He fears that if his daughter brings the ransom alone, both of them may be killed to eliminate witnesses.
